articles.title: Remembrance Sunday services planned across Rochdale borough
articles.excerpt: Residents will gather on November 8 to honour those who served in the armed forces, with parades and services in multiple towns.
articles.content_html:
Residents across the Rochdale borough are set to come together on Sunday, November 8, to pay their respects to those who have made sacrifices defending the country. Remembrance Day commemorations will feature a series of services and parades in towns including Rochdale, Castleton, Heywood, Littleborough, Middleton, Milnrow, Norden, and Wardle.

The events will see representatives from the Navy, Army, and Royal Air Force join veterans and civic dignitaries. Each service will include hymns, prayers, the Last Post, a two-minute silence, and the national anthem, ensuring a solemn tribute to those who served.

In Heywood, the parade will commence at 10.15am on Tower Street, proceeding to St James’ Street before arriving at Heywood Memorial Gardens for a service at 10.55am. Similarly, in Middleton, the parade will gather at 10.10am facing the Harbord Harbord pub, departing for Middleton Remembrance Gardens at 10.20am, with the service starting at 10.45am.

In Rochdale, participants will assemble outside The Flying Horse Hotel in Packer Street at 10.30am, where they will be joined by ward councillors and other civic guests. The parade will march to the Cenotaph for the service at 10.55am, followed by a march past before returning to The Flying Horse Hotel.

articles.title: Rochdale station regeneration scheme progresses with new homes and public square
articles.excerpt: A significant regeneration project around Rochdale railway station is underway, featuring new homes and a public square, aimed at improving access to the town centre.
articles.content_html:
A regeneration scheme aimed at transforming the area around Rochdale railway station is making significant strides, according to local officials. The project includes the construction of 81 new homes on vacant land adjacent to Rochdale’s Central Retail Park, part of a broader initiative to enhance connectivity between the train station and the town centre.

The development, named John Rennie Place in honour of the Scottish civil engineer who designed the Rochdale Canal, began in November 2026 and is expected to be completed by December 2027. The homes will consist of two, three, and four-bedroom properties and are being built as affordable net zero homes, marking a significant step in sustainable housing for the area.

In addition to the residential units, the regeneration plan includes the creation of a new public square in front of the station and 33 apartments on a brownfield site at the corner of Maclure Road and Station Road. This initiative is part of a larger effort to reconnect the station, which historically served as a hub for industrial transport, with the town centre, reflecting the changing needs of the community.

The project was made possible by a successful bid for £15 million from the government’s Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund, which has enabled the local authority to move forward after years of planning and investment challenges. The local council reports that the development is already benefiting the local economy and community, providing much-needed housing and improving public spaces.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The scheme to regenerate land around Rochdale station progressing | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch The scheme to regenerate land around Rochdale station progressing George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 24, 2026 | 9:23 AM Print A scheme which would transform the gateway into Rochdale is making significant progress, town hall bosses say. Some 81 two, three-and four-bedroom homes are currently under construction on vacant land next to Rochdale’s Central Retail Park. This forms part of a wider scheme to create a connection between the train station and the town centre. The wider regeneration of the area around Rochdale railway station also involves the creation of a new public square in front of the station and 33 new apartments on a brownfield site on the corner of Maclure Road and Station Road. The train station in Rochdale was once a hub for industrial business generations ago, so the distance between the station and the town centre was purposeful separation. But as times changed, society changed and the station suddenly started transporting people, not goods. This is why there is an idea to improve access and avenues from the station and the main hub of the town. This 81-home development, known as John Rennie Place, in honour of the late Scottish Civil engineer who masterminded the Rochdale Canal, got under way in November last year, and is due for completion in December 2027. The project, approved years ago, was unlocked following a successful bid for £15m from the government’s Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund. The transformation has been on the cards for a long time, but the local authority struggled to get the investment until last year. The properties will be the first affordable net zero homes delivered as part of a housing scheme supported by the council. The local authority says the development is already delivering benefits to the local economy and community. Contractor Willmott Dixon, working on behalf of the council, has already spent £3.3m with local civil engineering firm, Hovington Ltd, and supported a total of 95 weeks of apprenticeship and T-Level training, including three T-Level placements from Hopwood Hall College. Seven local people are also employed on the project, including two people who were previously unemployed, with the council’s work and skills team supporting the recruitment. Tommy Patterson, 22, from Middleton, is one of the local people working on the new homes. He said: “I had been out of work for six months when the job centre arranged for me to get my CSCS card and that led to me securing a scaffolding apprenticeship here on site. I have always worked and had been let go, so getting this job was a lifeline. “I live on my own and I was struggling to pay my bills. It’s great to work here. Everyone is lovely; it’s a smashing team.” Daniel Fletcher, 17, is studying for a T Level in design, surveying and planning at Hopwood Hall College, said: “I really like it here. I’ve been talking to the different trades delivering this project, so I’ve been exposed to different parts of the job, and I have the freedom to go onto site on my own. It’s already changed massively since I started in the summer.” The project is being led by Rochdale Development Agency (RDA) on behalf of Rochdale Borough Council. Councillor Danny Meredith, cabinet member for housing and regeneration at Rochdale Borough Council, said: ”We want local people and businesses to feel the benefit of local projects and it’s great to see that these benefits are already being felt on this development before a single house has even been completed. “By ensuring that social value is embedded in our procurement system, we’re making sure that local people are invested in the extensive regeneration which is taking place on their doorstep and are benefitting from the economic transformation we’re spearheading across the borough. That’s how it should be and how it will continue to be.” Work to create 142 apartments next to the new homes is ongoing, with the procurement of a delivery partner expected to get underway soon. articles.title: Community efforts revive historic Lodge Mill after devastating fire
articles.excerpt: Lodge Mill in Middleton, a historic site dating back to 1850, is seeing a revival thanks to community support following a fire that left it in ruins.
articles.content_html:
Lodge Mill, one of the oldest mills in Middleton, is undergoing a revival after a devastating fire left the historic structure nearly destroyed. The fire, which occurred earlier this year, resulted in the loss of significant parts of the mill, including a children's dance studio and an ice cream parlour. Fortunately, no injuries were reported during the incident.

The mill, which dates back to around 1850, was deemed uninsurable following the fire, complicating efforts for its restoration. However, local residents and volunteers have rallied together to support the rebuilding efforts. A GoFundMe page was established, raising over £7,000 to aid in the restoration process, demonstrating the community's commitment to preserving this historic landmark.

Martin and Paula, who were actively working on renovating the three floors above Lodge Mill prior to the fire, are now at the forefront of the recovery efforts. Thanks to the dedication of volunteers, life is returning to Lodge Mill, with plans to restore it to its former glory.

The revival of Lodge Mill is significant not only for its historical value but also for the community spirit it embodies. As restoration efforts continue, the mill is set to become a focal point for local activities once again, highlighting the importance of community involvement in preserving local heritage.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The potential return of Lodge Mill | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch The potential return of Lodge Mill George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 24, 2026 | 2 hours ago Print Community effort to clear up rubble at Lodge Mill in Middleton Lodge Mill in Middleton was devastated by a fire six months ago. Now there is hope for its future thanks to some dedicated business owners, volunteers and one avid ice cream fan. In March, firefighters were called to the massive blaze that left businesses in tatters and left the historic mill a shell. Several businesses were based on the ground floor of the building, believed to be one of the oldest mills in Middleton. A children’s dance studio, an ice cream parlour, a tea room, a dog chiropractor business and the Engine House event space, which held weddings, functions and parties, were all lost in the fire. The former silk and cotton mill, on Townley Street, dates back to around 1850. It was bought by couple Martin Cove and Paula Hickey in 2019, who were working passionately to renovate the three floors above. The pair have since kickstarted a fundraising campaign to restore the building soon after the fire, because the mill was uninsurable. Martin and Paula said the blaze ’caused the almost total loss of the main mill structure’. “No one was injured, and for that we are incredibly thankful,” the couple said at the time of the fire. “But we are heartbroken at the loss of not only our beloved Lodge Mill, but also the homes of the many local businesses and the community space we had all built together. “The outpouring of love and compassion from the people of Middleton and the surrounding area has given us the strength to carry on.” The GoFundMe page has raised just over £7,000 since it was launched six months ago. Thanks to a group of keen volunteers, life has returned to the mill. Rubble has been moved from the old Engine Room and more than 120 pallets of full bricks, Yorkshire Stone and specialty bricks have been picked up by hand and stacked. The annual duck race was held at the site in May, the ice cream shop has reopened and there are upcoming events for Halloween and Christmas. There is a long-term vision to bring the mill back into proper use again, with businesses on the ground floor and new flats above. But before that can happen, the site needs to be cleared. One keen volunteer is Dawn Alker, she visited The Ice Cream Shop at Lodge around eight years ago. She has returned many times since, but most recently as a volunteer. She said: “I went there for ice cream about seven or eight years ago and fell in love with the place. When it burnt down they asked for volunteers to clean it up. “Everyone goes down and chips in and does what they can on the day. “I used to be a manager in the NHS and now I am making a monster for Halloween in a burnt down mill. “It’s really nice to be working collectively. It’s turned into a community support project in a way. “I have mental health issues and I had stopped going outside and stayed inside too much. I started helping, selfishly, because I wanted the ice cream place back open again. “My mental health started to improve as I got moving more and others have said the same. “In terms of the project we have got to clear the site because it was bulldozed. Then the end goal is to rebuild it. “Then we want small businesses with flats over the top of them. That is just a vision at the moment. “It is going to  be a long project but it is going to be brilliant.” Dawn went on to say that the managers of Lodge Mill, Martin and Paula, have already instructed architects and looked at the structural integrity of the remaining walls at the mill. The business owners are hoping to submit planning proposals to the council in the coming months. articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council awards £1.1 million contract for young people's accommodation
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract worth over £1 million to Stepping Stone Projects for a new supported accommodation service for young people at risk of homelessness.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract valued at £1,108,081 to Stepping Stone Projects for the Rochdale Team Around the Young Person Accommodation Model (TAYPAS). This initiative aims to provide supported accommodation for young people aged 18 to 25 who are at risk of or experiencing homelessness. The contract will run from November 2, 2026, to November 1, 2029.

The TAYPAS model will deliver specialist, psychologically informed support within a newly developed, purpose-built facility that will feature 28 self-contained units. The service will offer 24/7 support and management, ensuring that young residents receive the assistance they need to transition into independent living.

This development is significant for the local community as it addresses the pressing issue of youth homelessness in Rochdale. By providing a safe and supportive environment, the council aims to improve the life chances of vulnerable young people in the area, helping them to build skills and confidence.

The next steps involve the construction and operational setup of the accommodation, which is expected to be completed in the coming months. This initiative not only reflects the council's commitment to supporting young people but also highlights the importance of addressing homelessness in the borough.

articles.title: From six modems to 580 staff: Rochdale’s Zen Internet puts people and planet alongside profit
articles.excerpt: Rochdale’s Zen Internet grew from £5,000 and six dial-up modems into a national broadband provider. Its B Corp approach puts customers, staff and the environment alongside profit.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale broadband business that began with £5,000 and six dial-up modems is highlighting how its B Corp approach shapes decisions about customers, staff and the environment.

Zen Internet was founded in 1995 after a conversation over a couple of pints between brothers Richard and Daniel Tang. Today, the company employs 580 people and supplies connectivity to homes and businesses across the UK.

Alongside that growth, Zen has retained its independence. Founder and chief executive Richard Tang remains its sole shareholder and has pledged never to sell the company.

What does being a B Corp mean?

Zen became a Certified B Corporation in 2020, joining a movement of businesses assessed against B Lab’s standards of social and environmental performance, transparency and accountability.

For Zen, that means considering the impact of its decisions on employees, customers, communities and the environment alongside financial performance.

The company points to practical examples, including two paid volunteering days each year for every employee, a fully UK based customer service team and a Contract Price Promise offering no mid-contract price rises.

Its community support includes donations to charities chosen through staff votes, involvement in the Rochdale Ambassadors scheme to attract investment and support for Rochdale Circle, which helps older residents live independently.

Zen also says it reinvests profits in its network and services, uses 100% renewable energy and refurbishes routers to extend their working lives and reduce waste.

One sourcing decision involved choosing an alternative to planned solar panels after identifying modern slavery concerns in the supply chain, despite the additional cost.

A business built for the long term

Tang says the company’s independence gives it freedom to make decisions with lasting benefits.

“From the moment I started Zen, I wanted to build a company that made a positive difference to the wider world, not just the bottom line,” he said.

“Becoming a B Corp was a natural fit given our freedom to make long-term choices, like keeping our support team in the UK and never raising prices mid-contract, that a purely shareholder-first business might struggle to justify.”

For Rochdale, Zen’s story is also one of a locally founded company growing into a national provider while continuing to employ hundreds of people.

For customers, the practical questions are straightforward: how much will a service cost over the full contract, who will answer when something goes wrong, and what happens to equipment when it is replaced?

Zen’s approach puts those everyday concerns at the centre of its business story.

articles.excerpt: Councillors have rejected a proposal for a 17-storey tower block beside the Grade II-listed Marble Arch pub in Manchester, citing concerns over its impact on the historic site.
articles.content_html:
Plans for a 17-storey tower block next to the historic Marble Arch pub have been rejected by Manchester City Council's planning committee. The proposal, submitted by The McGoff Group, aimed to construct 153 flats adjacent to the Grade II-listed pub on Rochdale Road, which has been serving customers since 1888.

The pub's owners expressed concerns that the development would threaten its future, describing the proposed building as "overbearing and oppressive". Councillor Jon-Connor Lyons voiced his worries about the potential impact on "one of Manchester's distinctive and much-loved historic pubs", highlighting the importance of preserving the pub's setting.

In addition to the concerns raised about the Marble Arch, councillors noted the absence of affordable housing in the proposed development as a significant factor in their decision to refuse the application. The committee's rejection reflects a growing awareness of the need to balance urban development with the preservation of historical sites.

This decision is significant for local residents and businesses, as it underscores the importance of maintaining the character of the area while addressing housing needs. The Marble Arch pub remains a key landmark in the community, and its protection is seen as vital for preserving local heritage.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Rejects Takeaway Application on Health Grounds
articles.excerpt: Plans for a new takeaway at 159 Yorkshire Street in Rochdale have been rejected by the council due to concerns over public health and the existing number of fast-food outlets in the area.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has refused an application for a new takeaway at 159 Yorkshire Street, citing health concerns related to the high number of existing fast-food establishments in the area. The proposal, submitted by Sheeraz Ahmed, aimed to convert the former Ria Money Transfer shop into a takeaway primarily focused on collection and delivery.

The application detailed plans for a business serving a variety of hot food products, including burgers, fried chicken, pizzas, kebabs, desserts, waffles, and milkshakes. It included internal alterations to create customer serving areas, food preparation spaces, and cooking facilities. The proposed opening hours were set from 11am to 11pm, and the establishment was expected to create four new jobs.

However, the council's planning officer raised concerns regarding the potential impact on local eating habits. The Public Health officer noted that the application would increase the availability of food high in fat, salt, and sugar. Furthermore, it was highlighted that a health impact assessment had not been conducted, leading to the recommendation that the development should not be approved.

This decision reflects ongoing efforts by Rochdale Council to manage the proliferation of fast-food outlets in the town centre, aiming to promote healthier eating habits among residents. The refusal of this application may influence future proposals for similar establishments in the area.

articles.title: Martlet Kitchen in Rochdale wins prestigious international award
articles.excerpt: The Martlet Kitchen, located in Rochdale Town Hall, has been awarded the Tripadvisor Travellers’ Choice Award for 2026, recognising its commitment to quality and customer satisfaction.
articles.content_html:
The Martlet Kitchen, situated within the historic Rochdale Town Hall, has received the prestigious Tripadvisor Travellers’ Choice Award for 2026. This accolade is granted to establishments that consistently earn positive reviews from customers, placing them among the top 10 per cent of listings on the popular review platform.

Opened in 2024 and led by chef Darren Parkinson, who trained at Hopwood Hall College, the restaurant has quickly established a reputation for serving high-quality British cuisine. Parkinson, who has previously worked at notable venues such as Shibden Mill Inn in Halifax and the Fleece Inn in Ripponden, emphasised the importance of using local ingredients, sourcing supplies from nearby businesses like Jacksons Farm in Milnrow and Defiance Distillery at Spotland Mill.

Restaurant manager Sarah Crabtree highlighted the team's dedication to providing a consistent dining experience, noting that the menu is regularly updated while retaining classic dishes like fish and chips. The Martlet Kitchen offers breakfast and lunch services, along with a grill club on Fridays and fine dining on Saturday evenings. Additionally, private dining options are available in the Mayor’s reception room at the Grade I listed town hall.

This award not only recognises the hard work of the Martlet Kitchen team but also enhances the profile of Rochdale as a destination for quality dining. As the restaurant aims for further accolades in the future, local residents and visitors alike can look forward to enjoying a dining experience that prioritises excellent service and locally sourced ingredients.

Published: 22 October 2026 Rochdale Town Hall’s Martlet Kitchen has picked up the Trip Advisor Travellers’ Choice Award 2026, placing it among the top-rated restaurants in the world on the popular review site. The award honours businesses which consistently receive great reviews, with their scores placing them in the top 10 per cent of all establishments registered on the popular review site. With millions of businesses from around the globe listed on the site, the award is a huge accolade for the Martlet Kitchen, which recently celebrated its second birthday. It’s not the first time the restaurant, which specialises in traditional, high-quality British food, has been lauded. In his food column for The Guardian, legendary food critic Jay Rayner, described the Martlet Kitchen as a ‘victory of professionalism, good sense and, most of all, great taste and skill’ when he visited shortly after its opening in 2024. The Martlet Kitchen is helmed by multi award winning chef, Darren Parkinson, who trained at Hopwood Hall College before working at acclaimed establishments including Shibden Mill Inn in Halifax and the Fleece Inn in Ripponden, both of which boast 2 AA rosettes. Rooted in the community, its food and drink is sourced from the local area, including Milnrow’s Jacksons Farm, Defiance Distillery at Spotland Mill and Grandpa Greene’s in Oldham. Commenting on the win, Darren said: “This award is great news and we’re aiming for more accolades in the future. It’s about good old fashioned British grub, cooked to perfection, using top quality local ingredients, coupled with excellent service.” Restaurant Manager, Sarah Crabtree, said: “I’m so proud of what we’ve achieved. I think one of the keys to the Martlet’s success is that we change the menu regularly to keep it fresh and seasonal, but we also keep the old favourites that people particularly enjoy, like fish and chips. Everyone who works here takes huge pride in their job, so the experience for the customers is really consistent. You know you will get excellent service and food every time you come in.” As well as breakfast and lunch, the Martlet Kitchen offers a fine dining experience on Saturday nights and a Friday grill club. The venue’s unique setting in the Grade I-listed Rochdale Town Hall has also enabled it to offer unique experiences, with a recently launched private dining offer giving guests the chance to dine in the Mayor’s reception room. Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and culture, said: “When we spearheaded the restoration of the town hall, with the support for the National Lottery Heritage Fund, we wanted every part of its operation to live up to this building’s grandeur and The Martlet Kitchen has delivered this in spades. articles.title: Chris Cheap appointed managing director of Northern Gateway regeneration in Bury and Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Chris Cheap has been appointed managing director of the development corporation overseeing the Northern Gateway regeneration programme, which aims to enhance infrastructure and housing in Bury and Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
Chris Cheap has been appointed as the managing director of the development corporation responsible for the Northern Gateway regeneration programme, which spans Bury and Rochdale. This initiative aims to coordinate the development of new homes, employment spaces, and infrastructure improvements in the area.

Mr Cheap joins the Atom Valley Northern Gateway Mayoral Development Corporation after nearly 23 years at Avison Young, where he led the UK transactional team. His extensive experience in real estate is expected to be pivotal in driving the regeneration efforts forward. He stated that successful delivery will require collaboration between public and private sectors.

One of the key projects under the Northern Gateway programme includes enhancing road connections to the M66 and M60 motorways, which is intended to facilitate further development and improve traffic flow in the region. This project is part of a broader strategy to boost economic growth and infrastructure in the Atom Valley Mayoral Development Zone, which also includes areas of Oldham.

The appointment of Mr Cheap is seen as a significant step towards revitalising the local economy and improving living conditions in Bury and Rochdale. As the project progresses, local residents and businesses can expect updates on developments and opportunities arising from this regeneration initiative.

articles.title: Rochdale house prices rise to £211,000 in August 2026
articles.excerpt: The average house price in Rochdale increased by 3.3% over the past year, while private rents saw a significant rise of 8.8%, according to the latest figures from the Office for National Statistics.
articles.content_html:
The average house price in Rochdale reached £211,000 in August 2026, reflecting a 3.3% increase from the previous year, according to data released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). This rise is notably higher than the average increase of 2.2% observed across the North West during the same period.

In addition to house prices, private rents in Rochdale also saw a substantial increase, with the average rent climbing to £859 in September 2026. This marks an annual rise of 8.8%, compared to £790 in September 2025, again outpacing the North West's average increase of 5.7%.

For first-time buyers, the average price paid for a home was £191,000 in August 2026, which is a 3.4% increase from the previous year's average of £184,000. Homes purchased with a mortgage had an average price of £215,000, also reflecting a 3.3% rise from £208,000 in August 2025.

These figures indicate a continuing trend of rising housing costs in Rochdale, which may impact affordability for local residents. The ONS advises that local housing data can be more variable due to the smaller number of properties involved, and they recommend looking at trends over a longer period for a clearer picture.

articles.title: Venus Lounge in Heywood wins Restaurant of the Year at National Curry Awards 2026
articles.excerpt: The Venus Lounge has been awarded Restaurant of the Year at the National Curry Awards 2026, recognising its contribution to the UK curry industry.
articles.content_html:
The Venus Lounge, a local restaurant in Heywood, has been awarded Restaurant of the Year at the prestigious National Curry Awards 2026. The awards ceremony took place yesterday at the House of Lords, celebrating the best in the UK's curry industry.

Organised by the Asian Catering Federation, the National Curry Awards highlight talented chefs and restaurants across the country. The Venus Lounge received a crystal trophy in recognition of its excellence and popularity among diners.

In a statement following the award, the Venus Lounge expressed gratitude to its customers for their support and for voting for them. The restaurant's success reflects its commitment to quality and service in the competitive culinary landscape.

This recognition not only enhances the reputation of the Venus Lounge but also contributes to the local dining scene in Heywood, attracting more visitors and curry enthusiasts to the area.

In September 2025, the claimant count was slightly lower at 8,625, indicating a year-on-year increase in unemployment claims. The latest figures were published by the Office for National Statistics through Nomis, and the September data is provisional and subject to revision.

The rise in claimants may reflect broader economic challenges affecting the local job market, although specific reasons for the increase have not been detailed in the report. The data is crucial for understanding employment trends in the area and may influence local policy decisions.

articles.title: Rochdale Council addresses concerns over local pub closures
articles.excerpt: Councillor Richard Jackson has raised concerns about the future of local pubs in Littleborough after the closure of The Wheatsheaf, highlighting restrictive covenants that hinder reopening efforts.
articles.content_html:
The future of local pubs in Littleborough is under scrutiny following the recent closure of The Wheatsheaf. This closure has sparked community outcry and raised concerns about the viability of pubs in the area. Councillor Richard Jackson addressed these issues during a Rochdale council meeting on October 15, highlighting the challenges posed by restrictive covenants that prevent former pubs from being reopened as such.

Councillor Jackson noted that approximately 50 per cent of pubs are owned by breweries or large pub companies, which often include covenants in sales to deter competition. This practice has led to a significant number of closures, with many pubs being sold off for alternative uses. He cited the example of the former Royal Oak pub, which closed in 2015 and was subsequently converted into a vape shop, a change that was later halted by Trading Standards due to regulatory issues.

The council's discussion aims to address the ongoing loss of pubs in the community, with Jackson's motion seeking to reduce the impact of these covenants. He expressed concern over the cycle of tenant attrition that many pubs face, stating, "We have seen this at the former Royal Oak pub. This was sold with an anti-competition covenant."

The implications of this discussion are significant for local residents and pub enthusiasts, as the council considers measures to protect these community assets. The outcome of this motion could influence future policies regarding the sale and repurposing of pubs in Littleborough and beyond.

Is the future of the local pub in danger? That’s the fear in Littleborough where the closure of another pub has sparked outcry. A few months ago The Wheatsheaf closed down in the Rochdalian town. There is strong community interest in reopening the pub as a local asset, but a small loophole means they fear they can’t do that. When breweries or large companies that own and operate pubs sell on the building, they can include a covenant that prevents it from being re-used as a pub. This covenant is inserted into a sale to stop competitors taking the pub on the cheap, the latest town hall meeting was told. Coun Richard Jackson brought forward a motion to Rochdale council to address this very issue to reduce the continued loss of pubs in communities. The Littleborough Lakeside councillor told the chamber on October 15: “The reality is that around 50 per cent of pubs are owned by breweries or large pub companies. They have a history of damaging the industry as a whole. This often leads to tenant attrition. “We are acutely aware of pubs being closed down after numerous tenants have left the building. The point of this motion is to address the churn. “We have seen this at the former Royal Oak pub. This was sold with an anti-competition covenant.” The former Royal Oak pub was closed down in 2015 and then sold off and became a vape shop, which was later shut down by Trading Standards. Coun Jackson called on the council to write to the government to block restrictive covenants on pub sales. He said that this loophole means most pubs get turned into shops or HMOs. His ward colleague Coun Tom Besford shared his annoyance that the future use of a community building can be dictated by the business interests of a brewery or company. The pair also credited Rochdale MP Paul Waugh for his continued work on this issue and raising it in Parliament. Speaking after the motion was passed in Rochdale Town Hall, Mr Waugh said: “This Government has already done the heavy lifting on pubs. Since August, the planning rules make it harder to turn a viable pub into flats or a shop, and the new Community Right to Buy gives people the power to buy their local. But one back door is still wide open. “A pub company can sell up and write into the deeds that the building can never sell another pint, and that ban binds every owner after them. Littleborough lost the Royal Oak that way, and I’m determined that we’re not going to lose the Wheatsheaf too. “The minister has asked for evidence, and with Rochdale council now behind us, I’ll be putting our town’s case to him directly.” It is a tough time for the pub industry nationally, with approximately one pub a day will have closed by the end of 2026, according to the latest figures from the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA).  The trade body estimates that around 360 pubs will permanently shut their doors by the end of the year. This is a free service and there is no need to register to use it. Terms and conditions apply (see link below), and guidance for developers is available. Terms and conditions Read the terms and conditions of using the data and images. About the data The data provides the food hygiene rating or inspection result given to a business and reflect the standards of food hygiene found on the date of inspection or visit by the local authority. Businesses include restaurants, pubs, cafés, takeaways, hotels and other places consumers eat, as well as supermarkets and other food shops. The data are held on behalf of local authorities participating in either the: national Food Hygiene Rating Scheme (FHRS) in England, Northern Ireland and Wales, or the Food Hygiene Information Scheme (FHIS) in Scotland Data for local authority areas running either of these schemes can be found on the Ratings site: See a list of local authorities running the FHRS or FHIS The scores part of the data is only applicable to scheme type FHRS (not FHIS) and are for hygiene, structure and confidence in management. These scores can be found in part 2 and 3 of Annex 1, A1.1 of the Food Law code of Practice . These scores are then used to calculate the food hygiene rating details of which can be found in the Guidance on implementation and operation of the Food Hygiene Rating Scheme: the Brand Standard and statutory guidance . When a rescore is uploaded by a local authority the scores of hygiene, structure and confidence in management will not be available in the data. Where the establishment is in operation from a private address the address and geocoding data may not be available. The LocalAuthorityBusinessID is provided by the local authority and is unique for that particular local authority data but could also be used by other local authorities. The FHRSID is system-generated and is unique in the data. It is based on the LocalAuthorityBusinessID and the LocalAuthorityCode . Where a new LocalAuthorityBusinessID is uploaded to the system by a local authority, a new FHRSID is generated. If a LocalAuthorityBusinessID is reused, for example for a new registration, the FHRSID will be retained for the establishment. Please note some local authorities use their database as a business database whereas others use an establishment database, therefore some local authorities will recycle the LocalAuthorityBusinessID where others will not. There are circumstances where the LocalAuthorityBusinessID and FHRSID may change, such as local authorities changing databases or where local authorities have merged. Details of where this has occurred can be found on the FHRS status page . Other useful information can be found on this page such as data types for fields. The business types and associated ID's can be found at: api1-ratings.food.gov.uk/business-types/xml Where Awaiting Publication is displayed instead of a rating, this is where the business has appealed their rating, and the local authority is in the process of determining the appeal. NewRatingPending is displayed as true in the data where a local authority has uploaded new data for an establishment which is not yet published as this data is in the notification or appeals period. It will be published after these time periods have elapsed. Where this is displayed as false, no new data is in the workflow to be published. Further information about the scheme can be found at https://www.food.gov.uk/safety-hygiene/food-hygiene-rating-scheme System status Status updates, usage advice and various other pieces of current information can be found at the System Status Page. API guidance for developers The API allows developers access to the underlying food hygiene rating data published at ratings.food.gov.uk . Developers can query XML files to return the geocoded data (longitude and latitude data are provided for food businesses). The XML data are updated daily and can be found below, grouped by local authority. Wales's local authority data can be output in English or Welsh. The API can also be used to query the live system (the data are automatically updated as local authorities upload and publish data) and return data in XML and JSON formats. Examples of how to use the API and information about the API can be found in the guidance document for developers: Read the API V1 guidance for developers (pdf 316KB, updated April 2024) Read the API V2 guidance for developers Images A set of hygiene rating images is available to be used with the API data. The images must only be used in accordance with the FHRS/FHIS Brand Standard and the terms and conditions . Number of results You can download up to 5,000 results by entering a number between 1 and 5,000 in the 'Number of results' field. If you need to download more than 5,000 results, in the 'Number of results' field enter 5,000, then enter each 'Page number' 1, 2 etc until all results are downloaded. articles.title: Emmerdale star Lisa Riley meets shoppers as Peacocks opens in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Peacocks opened its new Rochdale Riverside store on Thursday, with Emmerdale star Lisa Riley joining the celebrations and posing for photographs with shoppers.
articles.content_html:
Peacocks opened its new Rochdale Riverside store today, with Emmerdale star Lisa Riley joining the celebrations and posing for photographs with shoppers.

The actress helped officially launch the branch on Thursday 15 October, cutting the ribbon alongside store manager Claire Kershaw and the shop team. Riley also celebrated the visit on her own social media, confirming she had opened the new store.

Her appearance gave shoppers an opportunity to meet a familiar television face while exploring the retailer’s latest addition to Rochdale town centre.

Customers were keen to get through the doors, with the first shopper reportedly arriving at 6.30am. The first ten customers each received a £50 Peacocks gift card.

The new branch stocks clothing for women, men and children, bringing Peacocks back to the town following the closure of its former Wheatsheaf Shopping Centre shop in 2020.

For residents pleased to see the name return, today was a chance to browse the new shop, meet its staff and enjoy a little soap-star glamour alongside their shopping.

articles.title: Rochdale's Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre set to drive advanced manufacturing
articles.excerpt: The Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre at Kingsway Business Park marks a significant step for Rochdale's advanced manufacturing sector, with operations expected to commence in 2027.
articles.content_html:
A major milestone has been reached with the completion of the base build of the Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre (SMMC) at Kingsway Business Park in Rochdale. This 30,000 sq. ft facility is poised to become a key player in the UK's advanced materials and manufacturing sector, serving as a gateway for innovation and collaboration within the region.

The SMMC is the first significant development within the Atom Valley Innovation District (AVID), a 25-acre hub designed to foster advanced materials and manufacturing. The centre aims to bring together businesses, researchers, investors, and innovation partners, enhancing Greater Manchester's reputation as a leading centre for advanced manufacturing.

The completion of the building is the result of extensive collaboration among various stakeholders, including the Rochdale Development Agency (RDA), Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA), and The University of Manchester. The next phase will involve transitioning from construction to specialist fit-out, with the centre expected to commence operations in 2027.

Since the establishment of the Centre of Expertise in Advanced Materials and Sustainability (CEAMS) in 2023, over 90 companies have engaged with the initiative, benefiting from access to a national network of expertise and support. This development is expected to significantly contribute to the growth of the advanced manufacturing sector in Rochdale and beyond.

articles.title: Cozy Market in Milnrow shut down again for selling illicit tobacco
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Trading Standards has secured a three-month closure order for Cozy Market on Dale Street, Milnrow, following repeated violations involving the sale of illegal tobacco products.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Trading Standards has successfully obtained a closure order for Cozy Market, located at 79 Dale Street, Milnrow, due to the persistent sale of illicit tobacco products. The order was granted by Manchester Magistrates' Court and will see the shop closed for three months, marking the second time it has faced such action in recent months.

The latest closure comes just weeks after the shop reopened following a previous three-month closure order issued in June. During that period, evidence of illegal tobacco sales was secured by trading standards officers, prompting the court's decision to shut the establishment again.

Rochdale Council announced the closure on its Facebook page, reiterating its commitment to tackling the sale of illegal goods in the area. The law currently allows for a three-month closure for shops found selling illicit products, but there are plans to extend this period to a year, which could further deter such activities.

The repeated closures of Cozy Market highlight ongoing issues with illegal tobacco sales in the region. Local residents and businesses may notice a reduction in illicit goods being sold, contributing to a safer shopping environment. The council's trading standards team continues to monitor the situation closely.

articles.title: Rochdale Council announces new regeneration projects for Middleton
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has unveiled a series of regeneration projects aimed at revitalising Middleton, including the restoration of Hopwood Hall and the acquisition of Warwick Mill.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced a series of regeneration projects aimed at revitalising Middleton, following a recent High Court judgement in favour of the council regarding Hopwood Hall. This decision brings clarity to the future of the historic building, which has seen over £1.6 million invested since 2017 by the council and Historic England. The council is committed to funding essential repairs and considering options for its long-term future.

In addition to the Hopwood Hall project, the council has made significant strides in Middleton's regeneration ambitions. The acquisition of Middleton Old Grammar School is expected to lead to the announcement of a new tenant before the end of the year. Furthermore, the council is in the process of acquiring the long-derelict Warwick Mill, which could be redeveloped for new housing, enhancing the local community.

Plans are also underway to transform the Middleton Scout Hut into a community venue that will provide activities and training opportunities for young people. The council has also confirmed that banking and post office services will return to Middleton town centre in the new year, a move that is anticipated to provide a boost to the local economy.

These initiatives are part of the council's broader commitment to invest in the borough, creating jobs and driving economic growth. The council has also approved a £15 million support package over the next three years to assist residents facing financial difficulties, ensuring that help is available for those in need.

It's been a busy and productive few weeks across our borough, with positive news, exciting regeneration projects and innovative services making a real difference for residents in Heywood, Middleton, the Pennines, and Rochdale. I want to begin with Hopwood Hall. The council welcomed the recent High Court judgement, which found in our favour and brings much-needed clarity about the future of this important historic building. While it's disappointing that a lengthy and potentially costly legal process was necessary, we are now focused on moving forward. Since 2017, more than £1.6 million has been invested in Hopwood Hall by the council and Historic England, and we remain committed to funding essential repairs. Feasibility studies have been completed and options for its long-term future will be considered in due course. What is certain is that, once restored, Hopwood Hall will serve the wider Middleton community and continue to play an important role in the town's rich heritage. There has also been a significant boost for Middleton's regeneration ambitions, with a series of announcements demonstrating the momentum building behind the town's Mayoral Development Corporation. I'm delighted that Middleton Old Grammar School, recently acquired by the council, is expected to announce a new tenant before the end of the year. This follows news that the council is in the process of acquiring the long-derelict Warwick Mill, which could be brought back into productive use, including the potential development of new homes. Meanwhile, plans are progressing to transform Middleton Scout Hut into a vibrant community venue offering activities and training opportunities for young people. There is more good news on the horizon, with banking and post office services set to return to Middleton town centre in the new year. This is something I have long championed and it will provide another welcome boost for the town centre. These projects form part of our wider commitment to invest in every part of the borough, creating jobs, driving economic growth and ensuring our communities thrive. At the recent 'Our Town, Our Future' event, I saw first-hand the passion local residents, businesses and community groups have for Middleton and their determination to shape its future. It is an exciting time for the town, and we are turning ambition into action. Supporting residents through the cost-of-living crisis also remains a key priority. I am proud of the help we have provided through our Helping Hand campaign, which has supported thousands of older and vulnerable residents since 2022. As global economic pressures continue to affect household finances, the council has recently approved a further package of support worth around £15 million over the next three years through the Government's Crisis and Resilience Fund. This will provide emergency financial assistance, help residents keep their homes warm, debt and welfare advice, housing support, access to food provision and free warm spaces. We are committed to standing alongside residents who need support. This package will help reduce inequalities, ease pressure on household budgets and ensure thousands of people receive practical assistance throughout the autumn and winter months. My message is simple: if you need help, please get in touch. Further information is available at www.rochdale.gov.uk/costofliving or by calling 01706 923 685 . Finally, I want to highlight two important events that reflect our borough's strong and enduring support for the Armed Forces community. On Friday 16 October, Rochdale Town Hall will host a Festival of Remembrance featuring military music, marching bands, speeches, reflections and the Act of Remembrance. It promises to be a special evening and everyone is welcome to attend. Then, on Sunday 8 November, communities across the borough will come together for Remembrance Sunday services. It is always a poignant occasion, giving us the opportunity to honour and remember those who made the ultimate sacrifice in service of our country. For details of remembrance events across the borough, visit www.rochdale.gov.uk/events . Lest we forget. articles.title: Canine Country Club in Rochdale launches new classes after passing licence inspection
articles.excerpt: Canine Country Club has introduced new puppy sessions and enrichment classes following a successful animal activities licence inspection, enhancing its services for local dog owners.
articles.content_html:
Canine Country Club, located in Rochdale, has announced the launch of new puppy sessions and individual enrichment classes after successfully passing its first animal activities licence inspection. The owner, Stefanie, who recently took over the business, expressed her excitement in a message to customers, stating, "I am thrilled to share that we passed!"

The new puppy programmes will be held on Thursdays from 10am to noon, providing a structured environment for young dogs to learn and socialise. In addition to these sessions, the club will offer one-to-one enrichment classes designed for dogs that may be timid, less social, or older, allowing them to engage in activities in a quieter setting.

Stefanie emphasised that the welfare of the dogs is her top priority, stating, "Providing a welfare-focused program that prioritises the dogs' best interests has always been my top priority." This initiative aims to cater to the diverse needs of dogs in the community, ensuring they receive the attention and care they require.

Local dog owners interested in these new classes can contact Canine Country Club for further information and to book their spots. The introduction of these classes is expected to enhance the services available to pet owners in Rochdale, providing valuable opportunities for socialisation and enrichment for their dogs.

articles.title: Rochdale’s takeaway winning streak continues as Tandoori Flames takes North West title
articles.excerpt: Littleborough’s Tandoori Flames is the latest Rochdale borough business to take a regional ARTA title, following wins for River Beal in Milnrow and Wild Ginger in Littleborough last year.
articles.content_html:
First Milnrow, now Littleborough. The North West Takeaway of the Year award has found its way to Rochdale borough for the second year running.

Tandoori Flames, on Church Street in Littleborough, won the regional title at the Asian Restaurant and Takeaway Awards (ARTA), held at the London Hilton on Park Lane on Monday 12 October.

Last year's winner was River Beal Indian Takeaway in Milnrow. And that was not the borough's only success in 2025. Wild Ginger Restaurant in Littleborough also took the North West Restaurant of the Year award.

Three regional awards in two years, all earned by businesses in Littleborough and Milnrow. Not a bad record for the local curry scene.

The 2026 competition attracted more than 1,250 nominations from across the UK. Tandoori Flames and River Beal both appeared on the North West's ten strong takeaway shortlist, alongside businesses from Bolton, Manchester, Wigan and other parts of the region.

Tandoori Flames emerged with the title. The organisers say their judging process considered customer nominations, online reviews, food hygiene ratings and assessments by a panel of judges. That matters because the award is not based on a single enthusiastic recommendation, or merely on how many people happen to vote.

The Littleborough win continues a striking run for neighbouring communities in the borough. River Beal's 2025 title showed that a Milnrow takeaway could compete for regional honours. Wild Ginger's restaurant award in the same year gave Littleborough a victory of its own. Tandoori Flames has now brought another takeaway trophy back to the area.

The ceremony, hosted by presenter Samantha Simmonds and comedian Paul Sinha, brought together restaurateurs and hospitality professionals from around the country. Rochdale MP Paul Waugh was among the guests.

ARTA founder Mohammed Munim congratulated the winners and finalists and drew attention to the rising costs facing independent restaurants. Food, energy and staffing bills have all placed pressure on hospitality businesses, even where customer demand remains strong.

An award does not tell us everything about a restaurant or takeaway. Prices, consistency, service and personal taste still matter to customers. But these results provide a useful measure of how Rochdale businesses are performing beyond the borough.

And there is something pleasing about where the trophies have ended up. The awards cover a region with far larger centres of population and long established dining destinations. Yet, for two years, the takeaway title has gone to addresses in Milnrow and Littleborough.

Rochdale Daily congratulates Tandoori Flames on its 2026 win and recognises the achievements of River Beal and Wild Ginger in 2025.

Have you eaten at any of the three? Tell us what you rate on the menu in the comments. We are always interested in a good local recommendation.

articles.title: Queues form from 7.20am as SpudBros Express opens in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Early customers queued from around 7.20am for the new SpudBros Express outlet on Manchester New Road, with the first 100 customers promised a free loaded jacket potato at its midday launch.
articles.content_html:
Jacket potato fans were reported to be queuing from as early as 7.20am on Tuesday 13 October as SpudBros Express prepared to open its new Rochdale outlet.

The takeaway concession, at Manchester New Road, Rochdale, OL11 3PT, officially launched at midday with a promotion offering a free jacket potato to the first 100 customers through the doors. The reported 7.20am start would put some early arrivals more than four and a half hours ahead of opening.

Rochdale Daily received a report of large queues forming early in the morning. The precise number of people waiting has not been independently verified.

The Preston-founded SpudBros brand has built an enormous following online with videos of generously topped jacket potatoes. Its Express arm is expanding beyond traditional high streets through a partnership with food business Taster and forecourt operator EG On The Move.

The menu includes the Tram Classic, with garlic butter, a three-cheese mix, baked beans, crispy onions and Tram Sauce, alongside the Spudfather with chilli con carne, other loaded options and build-your-own potatoes.

The Rochdale concession is part of a wider plan to bring SpudBros Express to 30 EG On The Move roadside sites over three years. In an opening announcement, SpudBros co-founder Jacob Nelson said the Greater Manchester launch felt particularly special given the business's Preston roots.

According to the launch announcement, the new Rochdale outlet is expected to open seven days a week: 11am to 9pm from Sunday to Thursday and 11am to 10pm on Fridays and Saturdays. Opening-day trading began at noon.

More information about the menu and locations is available at the official SpudBros Express website, www.spudbrosexpress.com.

articles.title: Nominations open for Springhill Hospice's 2026 Man of Rochdale award
articles.excerpt: Springhill Hospice invites nominations for its 2026 Man of Rochdale award, recognising local volunteers. Nominations close on 2 November, with the winner announced at a luncheon on 27 November.
articles.content_html:
Springhill Hospice has opened nominations for its 2026 Man of Rochdale award, which celebrates volunteers who make significant contributions to the community. The award aims to recognise individuals who selflessly give their time to help others across the borough. Nominations will remain open until midnight on Monday, 2 November.

To be eligible, nominees must reside in the borough of Rochdale, be over 18 years old, and provide voluntary service for the benefit of the community. Individuals who have previously received a Royal Award, such as an MBE or OBE, are not eligible for this award. The winner will be announced during an awards luncheon at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday, 27 November, starting at 1pm.

Last year's recipient was a man who founded Re-Use Littleborough, a non-profit organisation that assists families in accessing essential items and supports children and communities overseas. In 2024, a man received the award after garnering over 40 nominations for his dedicated work with homeless and vulnerable individuals through the Good Solution Network and local charities.

This year marks the 32nd ceremony for the Man of Rochdale award, which is sponsored by Jackson Jackson and Sons, a local building and construction company. Tickets for the luncheon are priced at £65, with tables of ten available for £650. Proceeds from the event will support the hospice's care for adults with terminal or life-threatening illnesses and their families in Rochdale.

articles.title: Rochdale research centre moves closer to opening with £107m economic ambition
articles.excerpt: The Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre at Kingsway Business Park has completed its main building, with specialist fit-out ahead of a planned 2027 opening.
articles.content_html:
A new Rochdale facility designed to help turn scientific discoveries into commercial products has reached a construction milestone, ahead of a planned opening in 2027.

The main building of the Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre, at Kingsway Business Park, is now complete. Specialist equipment and facilities will be installed before it becomes operational.

The centre will support work on advanced materials with potential applications in medicine, electronics and construction, helping researchers test whether ideas developed in laboratories can become practical products.

Scientists and businesses will work with the University of Manchester and specialist innovation partners, connecting research expertise with the facilities needed to develop and manufacture new technologies.

The 30,000 sq ft centre is the first major physical development within the Atom Valley Innovation District, bringing researchers, manufacturers and investors together in Rochdale.

Independent analysis cited by the project’s partners forecasts £107 million in economic value over ten years, alongside opportunities to attract investment, businesses and skilled employment. That figure is a forecast, rather than income already generated.

Professor John Holden, the University of Manchester’s vice-president for civic engagement and innovation, said the next challenge was to connect the building with businesses, research and expertise to create lasting benefits.

For Rochdale, the centre represents a step towards establishing a larger advanced manufacturing sector—although its laboratories are still being prepared for the work ahead.

articles.title: ‘Really nice’: an editor’s visit to the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Daily's editor visited the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road with her little girl and found kind, efficient staff, a fully available menu and a welcome that earned a child's verdict: ‘really nice’.
articles.content_html:
There are plenty of ways to judge a new coffee shop. You can look at the menu, the speed of the service or whether it manages to make a quick stop feel pleasant. But after visiting the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road with my little girl, I found that the most telling review came from her.

“Really nice,” she said of the people working there. Two words, and a rather lovely assessment.

As the editor of Rochdale Daily, I spend a great deal of time looking at what opens, closes and changes across the borough. This time, rather than reporting on a launch, I wanted to experience the place as an ordinary customer — and a parent.

What stood out was the staff. They were kind, welcoming and efficient, handling our visit with the sort of ease that makes all the difference when you have a child alongside you. Good service does not need to be theatrical. Often, it is simply being treated warmly while everything runs as it should.

The full menu was available during our visit, too. There were no disappointing discoveries that something we wanted could not be ordered. It is a simple thing, but it matters: choice is only useful when the items are actually available.

The branch, which opened in August near Rochdale Infirmary and Dunelm, provides both indoor seating and a drive-through. For people visiting the hospital, passing along Whitworth Road or simply looking for a coffee stop, those options are convenient. But convenience alone is not what makes a customer want to return.

Children have an uncomplicated way of measuring an experience. They remember whether somebody was kind. They notice when they are made to feel welcome. My little girl did not care about the branding or the opening ceremony; she cared that the people were, in her words, “really nice”.

This was one family visit, not a claim that every visit will be identical. But the team deserve credit for getting the fundamentals right: kindness, efficiency and a menu we could actually order from.

Sometimes a new business makes its best first impression not through a grand announcement but through the people behind the counter. On our visit to Whitworth Road, Starbucks did exactly that.

articles.title: Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit highlights opportunities for local businesses
articles.excerpt: Businesses and organisations gathered at the Crown Oil Arena for the Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit, with discussions focused on accessing contracts, bidding and local economic growth.
articles.content_html:
Businesses and organisations from across the borough have come together for the Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit, with discussions focused on how local firms can access procurement opportunities and grow their businesses.

The event was organised by the Rochdale Development Agency and held at the newly refurbished Crown Oil Arena, home of Rochdale AFC.

The summit brought together organisations involved in procurement, regeneration and business support, including STAR Procurement, Match My Project, Hopwood Hall College, Willmott Dixon and the Rochdale Development Agency.

Discussions focused on how businesses can get onto the procurement ladder, understand the bidding process and position themselves to compete for contracts and opportunities with larger organisations.

Mayor Faisal Rana, who attended the event, said greater collaboration between local businesses and organisations delivering investment across the borough was important to ensuring local firms can benefit from upcoming opportunities.

He highlighted figures from the Rochdale Development Agency's latest independent economic impact assessment, which it says found that its work had created, supported or safeguarded 765 jobs and supported 699 businesses. The assessment also reported £14.30 in local economic value for every £1 invested.

The mayor also pointed to major investment programmes including Atom Valley, the Rochdale Rail Corridor, town centre regeneration, housing and skills investment as areas where businesses could potentially benefit from future procurement and supply-chain opportunities.

The summit comes as public-sector and regeneration projects continue to create demand for contractors, suppliers and other local businesses across a range of sectors.

The Rochdale Development Agency and organisations involved in procurement are encouraging businesses to understand the opportunities available and build their capacity to bid for work.

The event also underlined the potential economic impact of keeping a greater share of investment within the local economy, through jobs, business growth and local supply chains.

The Rochdale AFC Community Trust was also associated with the event.

A new independent bridal boutique has opened in one of Mytholmroyd’s historic buildings, bringing a fresh chapter of celebration to The Chapel on Scout Road.

Founded by Littleborough businesswomen Jessica Demain and Delphine Gott, Orla Bridal marked its launch on Saturday 3 October with a celebration attended by family, friends and local businesses who helped bring their vision to life.

Visits are private and by appointment only, giving each bride the space and personal attention to enjoy finding her dress with her closest guests.

Originally built in 1806, the Methodist chapel was extended to accommodate a Sunday school in 1872. Acquired by The Craggs Country Business Parks in 2018, it was sensitively restored and transformed into offices, preserving its heritage for a new generation.

Now, Orla is bringing something of the building’s original spirit back to its rooms: a place to gather, share meaningful moments and celebrate love.

For Jess and Delphine, that sense of occasion and belonging is at the heart of the business. Their vision is for every bride to feel comfortable, celebrated and free to be herself, surrounded by beautiful dresses in a calm and supportive setting.

Saturday’s launch offered guests a first look at the boutique, with flowers, fizz and cakes marking the culmination of weeks of preparation and support from local makers, tradespeople and businesses.

Orla Bridal is now welcoming appointment bookings at The Chapel, Scout Road, Mytholmroyd.

articles.title: One in seven Rochdale businesses could be overpaying business rates, research claims
articles.excerpt: More than 1,300 commercial properties in Rochdale could be paying too much in business rates, with potential overpayments worth a combined £2.9 million a year, according to BusinessRateChecker.com.
articles.content_html:
More than 1,300 commercial properties in Rochdale could be paying too much in business rates, with potential overpayments worth a combined £2.9 million a year, according to research from business rates intelligence company BusinessRateChecker.com.

The company's analysis examined 8,607 commercial properties in the borough and flagged 1,308 — 15.2% — as potentially over-assessed.

That was the highest proportion of any English local authority area included in BusinessRateChecker's analysis, ahead of Maidstone at 13.8%, Kirklees at 13.7% and Mid Suffolk at 13.7%.

BusinessRateChecker estimates the affected Rochdale properties could have grounds for reductions worth around £2.9 million collectively each year, equivalent to an average potential saving of approximately £2,217 for each property it identified.

However, the findings do not allege wrongdoing by Rochdale Borough Council.

The underlying rateable value of a commercial property is determined by the Valuation Office Agency. Councils then use the relevant rateable value and multiplier when calculating business rates bills.

Rupert Spiegelberg, CEO of BusinessRateChecker.com, told Rochdale Daily that businesses also have a responsibility to ensure the property information being used is accurate.

He said: “It is actually the responsibility of the property owner to update the VOA with changes in details of floor space, floor usage etc. Different RVs are applied to different spaces in a property. Many don't.”

He said larger companies were generally more likely to scrutinise their valuations because they had the resources to employ professional surveyors, while smaller businesses could be less likely to question what they were being charged.

He added: “Large businesses are usually quite up on this and will have the resources to hire surveyors to help them but for smaller businesses like hairdressers, coffee shops etc they tend not to question the bills as much.”

How Rochdale properties were assessed

BusinessRateChecker says its system compares the rate per square metre and zoning rates of individual properties with comparable nearby premises in the same category and valuation scheme.

It then examines factors including comparable rateable values and floor areas to identify properties whose valuations appear materially different from similar premises.

The company says tolerance bands are included to avoid flagging marginal cases.

Spiegelberg also told Rochdale Daily that the 1,308 figure could be an underestimate because some properties cannot be reliably assessed by its system.

Pubs are one example because valuations can depend partly on trading information which BusinessRateChecker does not have access to.

The company's own Rochdale dataset consequently records some properties as unassessable rather than assuming they are being charged correctly.

BusinessRateChecker currently analyses around 1.9 million commercial properties across England, using the published VOA rating list alongside other data to identify properties which may warrant further investigation.

Businesses can check their own property against comparable premises through the company's online checker.

articles.title: £12m plan aims to bring Storage World Middleton site back to life after devastating fire
articles.excerpt: A £12m rebirth bid has been launched for the Storage World site in Middleton, more than a year after a devastating fire destroyed the Old Hall Street facility.
articles.content_html:
A £12m bid to bring the Storage World site in Middleton back to life has been launched, marking a major potential investment in an important part of the town centre following last year's devastating fire.

The proposals concern the Storage World site on Old Hall Street, next to Middleton Arena. The former storage facility was badly damaged by a major blaze in June 2025, which burned for several days and led to demolition of the building. No injuries were reported, although customers and businesses suffered significant losses.

Place North West has reported that Storage World has now launched a £12m rebirth bid for the site. The move comes as regeneration work and planning for the wider Middleton town centre area continues.

Official Rochdale Development Agency updates show that the council and RDA have remained in discussions with Storage World since the fire. In June, the RDA said it was working with stakeholders to develop key principles for the area, including the potential to deliver improvements to Middleton Arena and create a new public space. It also confirmed that discussions with Storage World were continuing with input from Rochdale Borough Council's planning team.

The site is particularly significant because of its position beside Middleton Arena and within an area being considered as part of wider plans for the future of Middleton town centre. Earlier council reports said the outcomes of discussions over Storage World and the arena would feed into wider masterplanning work.

Before the fire, Storage World operated a large self-storage and workspace facility from Old Hall Street. The Middleton operation had previously expanded as demand grew, with the company providing traditional storage alongside space used by small and online businesses.

The 2025 blaze had a substantial impact on customers. Fire crews worked for days at the scene and parts of the building were demolished while firefighting operations were still under way to allow crews safe access. Storage World said at the time that its team was devastated by the impact on customers and the wider community.

The latest £12m proposal therefore represents a potentially significant next chapter for a prominent town-centre site and comes at a time when Middleton is the subject of wider regeneration and masterplanning proposals.

Rochdale Daily will update this story as further planning documents and details of the proposed redevelopment become publicly available.

articles.title: Rochdale brewery brings Retro Range of cask ales to The Baum this Friday
articles.excerpt: Coley's Brewery, now based at Fieldhouse Industrial Estate after previously brewing in Salford, will have three beers from its Retro Range pouring at The Baum in Rochdale this Friday.
articles.content_html:
A cask ale brewery now based in Rochdale is inviting local drinkers to sample three of its beers at The Baum this Friday.

Coley's Brewery has relocated to Fieldhouse Industrial Estate after previously brewing in Salford, bringing its cask ale production to Rochdale.

This Friday, three beers from the brewery's Retro Range will be pouring at The Baum, giving local real-ale drinkers an opportunity to try the Rochdale-produced beers in one of the town's best-known pubs.

The Retro Range is described by the brewery as a celebration of some of the most successful and recognisable beer styles of the past 60 years, combining traditional cask brewing with a deliberately nostalgic approach to British beer.

The brewery's owner is encouraging residents to head over to The Baum, say hello and support locally produced real ale.

The arrival of Coley's Brewery at Fieldhouse Industrial Estate adds another independent producer to Rochdale's food and drink scene and means beer brewed within the borough can now make the relatively short journey from the brewery to local pumps.

Independent breweries have played an important role in the revival of cask and craft beer across Greater Manchester, with pubs increasingly offering locally produced alternatives alongside national brands. For smaller breweries, getting beers onto pumps in established pubs provides an important opportunity to introduce their products to new customers and build a following close to home.

Three beers from Coley's Brewery's Retro Range will be available at The Baum in Rochdale on Friday 14 August. Availability will depend on stocks at the venue.

The event is for adults aged 18 and over. Please drink responsibly.
